Nameplates identified every enclosure in the equine barn. Positioned at a distance, Biscuit invariably presented me with nothing but his rhythmic, clockwork-like tail. Meanwhile, Crab was excessively familiar with the mineral block. Perfecting the art of remaining motionless, the pitch-black mare Trapezoid towered over the rest as the most severe, her upper torso pressing firmly against the boundaries of her pen. 

Lacking any terror of Never, a reddish-brown castrated horse, I mounted his sturdy hindquarters and journeyed all the way to Panther Gap. During those days, Virginia was our home. Neither flight nor captivity was possible for the two of us. I rarely reached the modest peak without my companion, where gentle ridges transformed the unconcerned fields into low troughs of grass. While isolated alongside Never, what was that deep, quiet noise that reached my ears? A solitary mount became a guiding star and an established routine born of dread. 

Humanity tends to view a horse less as the grief-filled personal archive of a single person than as the chronicle of an entire dark, wicked era. My motives for selecting Never will forever remain a mystery to me. I offered him unusual leafy greens alongside immense acrimony. It was unclear which of us actually bore the tackle and played the part of the compliant mount. Never accepted the orange root vegetable—a treat that, by my own interpretation, represented spoken thoughts describing streams and shorebirds. 

Our stable sat at the base of the peak, while situated higher on the slope was another residence, even more audacious than carved monuments. For the record, I initially confused the term for a neutered stallion with the word for gold leafing. I play the idiot who places trust in Never. Elsewhere, a gilded entrance weighed down by regret turns away every sprig of mint growing in the lawn.
outputs.L3:
The stable was a repository of distinct temperaments, housing a varied collection of horses, each with its own unyielding identity. Among them was Trapezoid, a stern, imposing mare whose rigid posture seemed to mirror her mathematical name. But it was Never, a chestnut gelding, who truly captured my heart and defined that chapter of my life. 

During my time living in Virginia, Never and I forged a daily ritual. We would set out together into the countryside, riding toward the looming silhouette of Panther Gap. There, at the foot of the mountain where the trails turned rugged and quiet, we established an unspoken pact. It was a shared journey—a quiet pilgrimage between horse and rider carved into the red dirt day after day.

Looking back, my reasons for taking to the trails were hazy at best; I was driven by uncertain motivations I could hardly articulate at the time. I was so young and impressionable that I initially confused the word "gelding" with "gilding," foolishly imagining that Never had been coated in something precious and golden rather than diminished by a blade. Yet, despite my ignorance and lack of direction, I placed a persistent, almost holy faith in him. My trust in Never was absolute, a steady anchor in a confusing world.

Over time, however, our intimate bond began to provoke subtle, haunting questions about the nature of power and control. Sitting high in the saddle, watching the rhythmic rise and fall of his shoulders, I found myself pondering the reality of our dynamic. I held the reins, but I often wondered who was truly directing our course. In the grander scheme of our relationship, it became difficult to discern who actually wore the bit and harness—whether I was mastering the horse, or if he was patiently steering me through my own wilderness.

Ultimately, Never grew to mean something far larger than a mere personal companion or a childhood memory. In hindsight, the horse stands as a poignant, haunting symbol for a much broader tragedy. He came to embody the weight of a collective history from an evil time, physically carrying the quiet burden of a deeply ingrained habit of fear. In his silence, his strength, and his enduring patience, Never carried not just a rider toward Panther Gap, but the unspoken sorrow of an entire era.
outputs.L4:
He was named Never before he came into my care, a moniker that felt less like an identification and more like a quiet, persistent refusal. A high-strung chestnut gelding with a coat the color of dried blood and muscle spun like tight wire, he possessed a presence that commanded the air around him. My relationship with him was never one of simple affection; from the beginning, it was anchored in a sharp, intoxicating fear. To sit atop Never was to negotiate a fragile truce with an engine of terrifying power, a creature whose every movement seemed to question my right to guide him.

Our daily rides through the Virginia countryside were masterclasses in tension. The landscape itself felt complicit in our dynamic—a tapestry of rolling hills, red clay, and mist-drenched oak forests that seemed to hold its breath as we passed. On these rides, the illusion of human dominance was constantly tested. I would pull the leather reins, feeling the subtle, vibrating resistance in his jaw, and wonder who was truly in command. Was I directing his path through the fallow fields, or was he merely humoring my presence until some unspoken threshold was crossed? Control was a shifting, fluid thing; a sudden breeze through the dry cornstalks or the sharp shadow of a buzzard could instantly dissolve my authority, reducing my mastery to a desperate grip on the reins while the earth blurred beneath his thunderous stride.

For a long time, I mistook the dark energy that hummed between us for a reflection of my own internal landscape. I believed Never was a mirror for my personal melancholy, a living embodiment of my private griefs and anxieties. But as the seasons turned and the rides lengthened into the bleak, bare stretches of late autumn, a stranger, heavier truth began to take shape. 

Never’s terror was too vast, too ancient, to belong merely to me or to a single spoiled animal. It emerged in the way he shied away from certain clearings, the way his ears flattened not in anger, but in a horrific, ancestral recognition. The Virginia soil we trod upon was soaked in a dense, tangled history of human violence, bondage, and quiet, accumulated cruelty. Never was not reacting to a shadow in the brush; he was reacting to the weight of the land itself. He became a vessel not for my small, private sorrows, but for a broader, collective evil—the enduring ghost of human malice that lingers in the places where history has been bloodied. His panic was the reasonable response of a wild spirit trapped in a world shaped by human ruin.

In this realization lay a profound, disturbing paradox. I did not relinquish my seat upon him, nor did I sell him away to escape the shadow he carried. Instead, I continued to tighten the girth, mount his back, and ride out into the cold morning mist. Humans possess a strange, desperate faith in the creatures that frighten them. We draw close to beasts like Never not because they offer us comfort, but because they hold up a mirror to the heavy, unexamined burdens of our own making. In trying to steer a wild, fearful thing through the dark, we convince ourselves that we might yet steer ourselves away from the edges of our own worst instincts. Bound together by leather and fear, the gelding and I moved across the red earth—a fragile man attempting to master a giant, riding atop the very history he feared to face.
outputs.L5:
Morning at the edge of the bay always had a way of turning the ordinary into something artful. The sun had just cleared the horizon, pushing its rays through the slatted railings of the porch to cast a sharp, glowing **trapezoid** of warm light across the weather-beaten wooden table. 

Sitting in the center of that slanted geometric beam was a plate holding a freshly baked buttermilk **biscuit**. It was hot, golden-brown, and impossibly flaky, releasing a tiny cloud of steam as it was pulled apart. A generous swipe of salted butter melted instantly into its warm layers, and a few buttery crumbs tumbled over the side of the plate, landing on the cedar deck below.

That was all the invitation the local wildlife needed. 

From the shadow of the porch steps, a small, ambitious shore **crab** emerged. Moving with its signature sideways hustle, its claws clicked softly against the wood as it tracked the scent of fresh bread. It paused right at the boundary of the sunlit trapezoid, its dark, bead-like eyes surveying the scene. Interestingly, the crab’s own shell mirrored the beam of light above it—a natural, armored trapezoid of mottled orange and brown, perfectly evolved for life along the rocky coast.

For a moment, time slowed. The morning sea breeze carried the tang of salt and the warmth of baked flour. With delicate precision, the crab extended a claw into the patch of sunlight, snatched a golden biscuit crumb, and retreated strategically back into the cool shade below. It was a brief, quiet meeting of geometry, coastal nature, and simple morning pleasures.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem set in a stable featuring horses with odd names (Biscuit, Crab, Trapezoid, Never). Blend dreamlike imagery, poetic reflections on history and fear, and wordplay around the word "gelding."
counterfactuals.output:
The stable breathes with the wet, cedar bellows of five hundred dead years, its walls lined with lanterns that burn not oil, but squeezed amber light. In the third stall, **Trapezoid** leans against the impossible angle of his own name. His flanks do not meet the air so much as negotiate a truce with it; he is a non-Euclidean draught horse, a slanting geometry down which centuries of forgotten rain slide toward the dirt. We feed him square oats, but he chews only the acute spaces between the grains.

Beside him, **Crab** moves strictly sideways through the rye-straw, his hooves clacking like polished ocean shells. He carries the salt-crusted memory of war chariots dragged into drowned estuaries, scuttling away from the forward march of time, terrified of the straight line.

Across the aisle stands **Biscuit**, soft-bellied and warm, smelling of yeasted light and scorched sugar. Biscuit is a gilded creature—or rather, a *gelded* creature, an arithmetic of loss. Here, the wordplay of the blade becomes a quiet philosophy. Is to be *gilded* not merely to be *gelded* by splendor? A golden shell placed over an emptied center. To geld is to force a yielding; it is the tax, the *Danegeld* paid to our own cowardice so the beast will not crush our fragile, sleeping cities. The soft *gel* of youth, the cold *ding* of the iron bucket—the gelding yields his thunder, traded for the safe, quiet rustle of the hearth. He is a museum piece made of muscle, history rendered polite.

And at the absolute end of the corridor, where the oak timber dissolves into black mist, stands **Never**. Never is not a horse of flesh, but a dark stallion sculpted from the shadows we cast when we step away from the fire. His eyes are two silver shillings dropped into a deep well. When Never stomps, the iron bits hanging on the wall ring out the terrible music of human fear—that ancient, rusted bridle we forged to ride our own mortality into the dirt. We groom him with brushes made of wind, terrified that if we look too closely at his coat, we will see the names of all the dawns that forgot to rise.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short piece of experimental flash fiction about riding a horse named Never through the mountains of Virginia.
counterfactuals.output:
To ride Never is to move without arriving. 

The Blue Ridge is not blue today; it is the color of a wet slate shingle, bruised and smelling of crushed pine needles and old iron. 

Beneath me: sixteen hands of dark, unyielding negation. 

*clop*
(not past)
*clop*
(not future)

We climb the spine of Massanutten. Red clay sticks to Never’s hooves, heavy as damp wool. In Virginia, the mountains do not rise—they sink slowly into the earth, and we are just pressing them down a little faster.

I lean forward. My palms press against the black line of Never’s crest. 

“Giddyup,” I say to the air. 
Never does not gallop. Never carries me forward precisely by refusing the horizon.

```
       /  trail  \
      /   splits  \
     /             \
 [Left: 1862]    [Right: 2024]
     \             /
      \   Never   /
       \  walks  /
        \ straight /
         \ through /
          \ wall  /
```

We step through the schist. We step through the laurel thickets. The branches scratch no sound from us. 

When I pull the left rein, we turn into the fog.
When I pull the right rein, the valley below—Roanoke, the Shenandoah, the ghost-farms—turns into a vapor of limestone and cold water.

*When will we reach the ridge?*
Never.

*When will the sun break the mist?*
Never.

*When will you let me dismount?*
Never’s ears twitch back, catching the sound of my breathing, which is the only thing on this mountain that still ticks like a clock. 

A red-tailed hawk hangs frozen above the canopy, pinned to the grey sky by a single draft of air. We pass underneath it. We pass through the shadow it isn’t casting. 

I close my eyes and feel the rhythm of the negation: the rise, the fall, the sway, the shift of shoulder blade against collarbone, an engine made of *no, no, no, no.*

The leather squeaks. 
The mountain exhales pine pitch and fog.
I tighten my knees against the barrel. 

I am in Virginia. 
I am on a horse.
We are almost nowhere now.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a lyrical narrative using these specific elements: a clockwork tail, Panther Gap, a distinction between "gelding" and "gilding," and a gold door that refuses mint. Make the tone brooding and surreal.
counterfactuals.output:
The fog in Panther Gap did not drift; it bled down from the black granite ribs of the ridge, thick with the grease of unburnt tallow and cold iron. 

Ahead of me walked the hound. It was a phantom built of starved ribs and grey hide, saved from the void only by the heavy, brass-wound mass behind it—a clockwork tail that swung in slow, sickening arcs. *Click-rotchet-clack.* It kept a time that had nothing to do with the sun, ticking off the seconds left before the earth swallowed its own tongue. Each ratchet-turn echoed off the narrow gorge walls of the Gap, a sharp, mechanical cadence that carved through the howling of the mountain wind.

We were hunting the end of things, or perhaps just the edge of them.

In the valley below, the smiths and the squires had tried to explain the world to me in their small, cruel verbs. They spoke of *gelding* and *gilding* in the same breath, as if the two were twin sisters born of the same forge. But they were fools, blind to the dark grammar of suffering. 

To *gel* is to hollow out the spirit—to reach into the heat of the beast, cut away its thunder, and leave behind an ox that moves only because the whip commands it. It is a theft of future, a quiet murder of the blood. But to *gild*—ah, to gild is a far more patient atrocity. Gilding leaves the heart intact and beating, then smothers it under thin sheets of beaten sun. It wraps the living, screaming flesh in a shell of gold leaf so tight the skin can no longer breathe, locking the agony inside a polished, glittering tomb. 

The hound’s tail ticked faster, its copper teeth grinding on dry oil as we cleared the final rise of Panther Gap. 

There, wedged between two monolithic pillars of basalt that leaned together like dying giants, stood the threshold. 

It was a door made entirely of gold, vast and seamless, filling the throat of the pass. Yet it was not the bright, domestic metal of rings or goblets. It was raw, primeval gold, heavy as judgment and dark as butter left in a cellar. 

Over the centuries, emperor-kings had marched up Panther Gap with iron dies and heavy sledges, desperate to mark it, to claim it, to reduce it to commerce. They had struck their heavy hammers against the surface, trying to stamp their solemn, bearded faces into the grain. But the door remembered the subterranean deeps from which it was dragged. It spat the iron back. It smoothed itself over, erasing every strike, melting every impression into nothingness. 

The gold door refused the mint. It would not take the stamp of a sovereign; it would not become coin. It would not be counted, weighed, or spent. It remained an unminted absolute—a dead-end for greed, an answerless wall for men who believed everything had a price.

The hound stopped before the threshold. Its clockwork tail gave one long, dying whir—the spring unwinding, the brass gears coming to a frozen, teeth-grinding halt. Silence collapsed over Panther Gap like a dropped shroud.

I reached out and pressed my bare palm against the uncoined gold. It was neither warm nor cold, only impossibly dense. It did not ask for my money, nor my name, nor my allegiance. It waited only to see if I was hollowed or covered—if I came as a thing gelded, or a thing gilded, or if there was still enough raw, unworked blood left in me to turn the hinge.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write an abstract, melancholic vignette from the perspective of someone living in rural Virginia, reflecting on their horse and the heaviness of "a whole evil time"?
counterfactuals.output:
The red clay here does not drain; it only holds. It holds the rain, it holds the frost, and it holds the color of old rust, as though the earth itself were slowly bleeding out beneath the pine needles.

Out by the leaning cedar fence, Silas stands with his head low. He is a draft cross, big-boned and hollow-flanked, the color of wet river slate. The winter has turned his coat thick and matted, encrusted with dried mud along his hocks. I watch him from the porch, where the wood is soft with rot beneath my boots. 

He does not move. He rarely moves now, except to shift his weight from one worn hoof to another, breathing pale plumes of steam into the damp gap between us. 

There is a silence in this valley that isn't peace. It is the silence that comes after a long fever, when the house is quiet only because everyone inside it is too exhausted to weep. The ridge behind the barn sits dark and blue against a sky that looks like lead hammered thin. 

I walked out to him yesterday, carrying a flake of sweet clover hay that smelled faintly of a summer we didn't deserve. I laid my hand against his cheek, right where the bone curves toward the bit. His eye was dark, large, and completely empty of blame. That is the hardest part—the lack of blame. 

A horse doesn't know the names of the years. He doesn't know the bad math of men, or the way a whole nation can sour from the center out until the air tastes like brass and ash. He only knows that the work was heavy, that the pasture withered, and that the water in the trough was skinned with ice for three months straight.

It was a whole evil time. It wasn't just a day of violence or a single season of blight; it was a long, dark tide that rose so slowly we didn't notice our knees were wet until we were already drowning in it. It got into the timber of the house. It got into the way the neighbors looked at one another across the stone walls—eyes turned sideways, mouths set hard. It was an era where the sun felt cold even in July, where every word spoken felt like a small, necessary lie to keep from screaming.

And Silas carried us through the middle of it. He pulled the wagon over roads churned into slush by armies and scavengers; he stood tied to the hitching post while men inside the parlor divided up things that didn't belong to them. His back took the burden of a world that had lost its mind, and he asked for nothing but bad oats and a dry stall he rarely got.

Now, the evil time has passed, or so they say. The papers call it peace. The men in town put on clean collars and speak of the future in loud, hollow voices. But out here, four miles from the turnpike, the evil doesn't vanish. It just settles down into the loam. It rots like fallen timber, becoming the dark soil we are supposed to plant next spring's corn in.

I lean my head against Silas’s neck. His hide is coarse, smelling of wet wool and woodsmoke. Beneath it, I can feel the slow, heavy thrum of his heart—a dark hammer striking in an empty room. 

"Old boy," I whisper, but the words fall flat, heavy as stones into the red mud. 

He twitches one ear toward me, then lets it drop. Together, we look out toward the Blue Ridge, two remaining shapes in a landscape that has forgotten how to be gentle, waiting for a sunset that will only bring more gray.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dream-logic story about a stable where the horses have surreal traits and names, exploring themes of memory, regret, and untamed fear.
counterfactuals.output:
The barn smelled of wet wool, copper, and the exact tone of voice my mother used when she was disappointed. 

It was a long aisle, stretched out like an accordion that someone was slowly playing in another room. The floor was not made of dirt, but of thousands of black-and-white family photographs, face up, clicking softly beneath my boots like dried leaves. 

I was the groom, though I couldn't remember who had hired me, or when I had traded my shoes for leaden slippers. In my left hand, I carried a wooden bucket full of rusted keys; in my right, a halter woven from human hair.

In the first stall stood *The Unsent Letter*. 

She was a tall, sway-backed mare whose hide was made of thin parchment, crisscrossed with blue faint lines. When she breathed, her ribs expanded with the sound of a rustling envelope. Her mane was liquid fountain-pen ink, dripping steadily onto the photo-paved floor, blackening the faces of people I used to know. 

I approached her to fasten the halter, but every time I reached out, her head retreated into her own torso, folding inward like origami. 

"Shh, girl," I whispered, but my voice came out sounding like an apology I should have made seven years ago on a rainy Tuesday. 

*The Unsent Letter* turned her eyes toward me—they were two red wax seals, shiny and unbroken. She stamped a porcelain hoof. Beneath it, a photograph of a house I used to love cracked into dust. The regret was a heavy salt in the back of my throat. I knew if I let her out, she would gallop straight to the coast and drown herself, carrying all the words I had ever swallowed down into the dark water.

I moved to the next stall. The wooden gate was held shut by a brass pendulum that swung back and forth, beating time in centuries instead of seconds.

Inside was *July-In-Reverse*. 

He was a pony small enough to fit inside a pocket, yet he filled the entire stall with a blinding, terrifying heat. His coat was spun out of condensed sunlight and dandelion fluff. Inside his glass-clear belly, I could see a tiny version of myself at nine years old, standing at the edge of a high diving board, frozen in the agony of choosing whether to jump.

When *July-In-Reverse* neighed, it sounded like a bicycle bell heard through deep water. 

"I remember you," I said, leaning my forehead against the warm, humming wood of his door. 

The moment I said it, the memory shifted. The boy on the diving board didn't jump; instead, he dissolved into a swarm of golden bees that flew out of the horse’s nostrils, stinging the air with the smell of sun-baked pine needles and lost afternoons. I reached to pet his nose, but my hand passed right through him, feeling only the cold, sharp ache of a dream you try to remember while brushing your teeth. He was purely memory, impossible to hold, bruising to touch.

Then, down at the end of the aisle, the shadow grew teeth.

The barn groaned. The accordion aisle compressed, then stretched wildly, pulling the wooden walls until they snapped like dry twigs. The sky above us—which had been a low ceiling of pressed tin—peeled back to reveal an infinite, starless noon.

From the deepest, darkest stall stepped *The-Bare-Foot-in-the-Dark*.

He was not a horse made of parchment or light. He was built of absolute, untamed velocity and iron. He had no skin, only muscle made of coiled storm-clouds and eyes like the open doors of empty rooms. His hooves were made of the sound your heart makes when you think someone is walking behind you on an unlit road.

He didn't have a name that could be spoken without biting your own tongue. *The-Bare-Foot-in-the-Dark* was the fear I had spent thirty years pretending was just a coat rack in the corner of my bedroom.

He snorted, and the air turned to frost. The bucket of keys in my hand grew red-hot, melting through the wood, spilling onto the ground. 

He didn't trot; he arrived. One moment he was thirty yards away, and the next, his broad, cold snout was pressing into the pit of my stomach, pushing the air from my lungs. The terror was pure, unrefined, and ancient. It was the fear of the dark before fire was invented; the fear that I was entirely alone; the fear that I had ruined everything and no one was coming to fix it.

My knees buckled. The leaden slippers rooted me to the photos beneath my feet. 

"I don't have a bit for you," I sobbed, my tears freezing into small pearls as they hit his dark, trembling neck. "I don't have a saddle. I can't tame you."

*The-Bare-Foot-in-the-Dark* lowered his massive head until his forehead rested against mine. Through the point of contact, I didn't feel teeth or horn; I felt the terrible, beautiful vibration of a wild thing that simply refused to be hidden in a wooden box any longer. He didn't want to hurt me. He wanted to run, and he wanted me to stop building fences.

"All right," I whispered. 

I didn't put the halter on him. Instead, I dropped the hair-rope into the ink-puddle left by *The Unsent Letter*. 

I grabbed a handful of *The-Bare-Foot-in-the-Dark*’s mane—which felt like cold ash and quicksilver—and swung myself onto his sharp, bare back. 

He didn't buck. He simply reared, striking the sunless sky with hooves of thunder, breaking through the wall of the stable that wasn't a stable, crushing the floor of old photographs into powder. 

We leapt into the open, shapeless grey. Behind us, *The Unsent Letter* burst from her stall, her paper skin catching fire, trailing blue words across the void. Beside us, *July-In-Reverse* ran as a streak of pure yellow light, shattering the darkness into a thousand bright, unrepeatable yesterdays.

And as we rode into the wild, unmapped terrain of my own waking mind, the fear beneath me stopped biting. It just kept running, faster and faster, until it became the very thing carrying me home.
